text.MAP1_RESULT: Dam gauges cluster where the big reservoirs are: California (53), the Pacific Northwest (50), the Mid-Atlantic (39) and the South Atlantic-Gulf (29). The Tennessee, Lower Mississippi and Souris-Red-Rainy regions have one each. 297 of the 314 controls come from their dam gauge's own region. New England ran out after 7 and California after 46, and the other 17 were matched on drainage area alone from any region, so California dam gauges got controls in Florida, Illinois and the Appalachians. West of the Mississippi (HUC 10 to 18) holds 171 dam gauges and 170 controls, the East 143 and 144.
text.MAP1_CONCLUSION: East against West, the controls sample the same climates as the dam gauges, and region by region they mostly do too. The 17 borrowed controls are the exception; they are hollow in Figure 2 and tagged in the table.
text.AREA_RESULT: The match held for small basins and failed for large ones. Below 500 km² the median control is the same size as its dam gauge and 88 % of pairs are within a factor of 1.5. Above 5,000 km² unregulated rivers that large are rare among the training gauges, and the median control is 0.15 times the size of its dam gauge. Overall the controls are smaller (median 724 against 1,225 km²); 47 % of pairs are within a factor of 1.5 and 57 % within a factor of 2. The 17 borrowed controls match area almost exactly.
text.AREA_CONCLUSION: Size could confound the comparison, so it was checked. A dam gauge's gain minus its control's gain is about the same in the 147 pairs matched within a factor of 1.5 (median +0.012, 95 % interval +0.003 to +0.030) as in the 167 that are not (+0.017, +0.005 to +0.034), and the controls' change in NSE does not track their area (Spearman ρ 0.06). The mismatch does not drive the results below. A rebuilt set should still let large dam gauges share controls or reach across regions.
text.F1_RESULT: Dam gauges: median change +0.017 (95 % interval +0.007 to +0.026), 210 up and 104 down; 73 gain more than 0.1 and 8 lose more than 0.1. Controls: median change 0.000 (−0.0004 to +0.0005), 155 up and 159 down; 12 gain more than 0.1. Gauge by gauge, a dam gauge beats its own control by a median of +0.014 (+0.007 to +0.028), ahead in 202 of 314 pairs (sign test p = 4e-7). The one-parameter plain bucket gets about half of the gain (+0.009 at dam gauges, 0.000 at controls). KGE does not improve: median change −0.002 at dam gauges and −0.002 at controls, since the fit maximises NSE.
text.F1_CONCLUSION: The bucket helps below dams and leaves the controls alone: at 185 of 314 controls the tuned response time sits on the grid floor of 0.05 days, which is pass-through. The gain is not generic smoothing. It is small for the typical dam gauge and large for about a quarter of them, and it lands where the no-dam model is worst (median no-dam NSE 0.27 at the 73 gauges that gain more than 0.1, against 0.60 at the rest). That is why the group median NSE rises from 0.526 to 0.601 while the typical gauge moves by 0.017.
text.MAP2_RESULT: Dam-gauge gains are largest in the dry West and on the flood-control reservoirs of the plains: median change +0.162 in the Rio Grande (8 gauges), +0.102 in the Upper Colorado (10), +0.078 in Texas-Gulf (4), +0.043 in the Upper Mississippi (19) and +0.032 in the Missouri (23). The Northeast, Great Lakes and Ohio gain little (+0.001 to +0.010). California is the exception: 53 dam gauges, median change 0.000, 23 up and 30 down. The control map is mostly hollow circles; its few large gains (South Fork Jocko River, Montana; Santa Fe River, Florida) are rivers where the no-dam model is poor to begin with (NSE −1.94 and −0.31).
text.MAP2_CONCLUSION: The pattern fits the hypothesis everywhere except California. 24 of California's 53 dam gauges sit below hydropower dams, and many Sierra projects route water through tunnels and powerhouses around the gauged reach. A bucket fed only by the natural inflow cannot take water out of the river, which is the likely reason it finds nothing to fit there. The learned release may need a diversion or loss term, or those gauges should be scored separately.
text.F2_RESULT: The dam median sits right of the control median in 15 of 18 regions. The exceptions are Tennessee and Lower Mississippi, with one dam gauge each, and California. Control medians stay within 0.01 of zero everywhere except three regions resting on one or two gauges (Lower Mississippi +0.06, Lower Colorado +0.05, Souris-Red-Rainy +0.03). The largest dam medians are the Rio Grande (+0.16), Lower Colorado (+0.16, 2 gauges), Upper Colorado (+0.10) and Texas-Gulf (+0.08).
text.F2_CONCLUSION: The dam effect is broad, not one region's doing, and it is strongest where storage is large against flow and the no-dam model is weakest. The Rio Grande's dam gauges have a median regulation of 2.9 and a median no-dam NSE of −0.11; the Ohio's have 0.17 and 0.80.
text.F3_RESULT: The median gain is +0.012 with storage up to a tenth of annual flow (46 gauges) and +0.012 from 0.1 to 0.5 (104), rises to +0.027 from 0.5 to 1 (76) and +0.030 from 1 to 2 (46), then drops to +0.004 above 2 (42). Dams on the gauge's own reach gain more (+0.020, 214 gauges) than dams further up (+0.011, 100), and gauges below a chain of large dams gain more (+0.024, 148) than gauges below a single one (+0.014, 166). Controls sit at 0.000. One point is clipped at the top: Rio Hondo below Diamond A Dam, New Mexico, goes from −17.5 to −11.2 on a channel that is dry 85 % of days.
text.F3_CONCLUSION: The gain grows with regulation up to about a year of storage and then collapses. The most heavily regulated gauges (Courtright, Eagle Nest, Monticello, Navajo, Boca, Stampede) sit below reservoirs that carry water across years, whose releases follow operating rules, demand and snowpack more than this year's inflow. A linear bucket with a seasonal response time cannot follow that, and at Courtright the fit ran into the 1,000-day wall. The release law needs a cap on T₀ and, for these dams, information beyond inflow.
text.F7_RESULT: Long Branch Dam (flood control, Missouri): the model's late-May storm peak of 41 m³/s is cut to 20 against an observed 31, and the recession is held up. That year's NSE rises from 0.72 to 0.88, and over all test years from −0.05 to 0.74, with T₀ 3.7 days. Agency Valley Dam (Oregon): the gauge runs near zero from November to mid-January while the reservoir fills (0.5 m³/s on average over October to January), where the model passes 2.7 m³/s. The fitted T₀ is half a day and the lines barely move (0.393 to 0.411 over the test years). Courtright (hydropower, California): the gauge records a small steady release of 0.2 to 0.7 m³/s. The fit put T₀ on the 1,000-day wall and used the seasonal term to release one smooth spring pulse, which misses (−1.62 to −3.47). Queets River, a control: T₀ sits on the 0.05-day floor and the ochre line covers the teal one (0.799 to 0.797).
text.F7_CONCLUSION: The bucket does what a flood-control reservoir does and nothing more. It cannot hold water for months and let it out on an operator's schedule (Agency Valley), and where the release has nothing to do with inflow, the fit falls back on the seasonal term alone (Courtright). Both failures point the same way: the release needs a bounded T₀ and some input besides the current inflow, such as storage state.
text.F8_RESULT: The viewer opens on the Kaskaskia River at Shelbyville, Illinois, below Lake Shelbyville (flood control, 256 MCM), in WY2008. The model passes storm peaks of up to 286 m³/s; the gauge records the reservoir's stepped releases, never above 102 m³/s. The tuned bucket (T₀ 29 days, swinging from 6 to 139 days over the year) holds its peak to 93 m³/s and follows the release levels, though not the steps. That year's NSE rises from −0.79 to 0.56, and over 1996-2010 from 0.290 to 0.666.
text.F8_CONCLUSION: A linear store with a seasonal response time gets the volume and timing of a flood-control release roughly right but not the operator's steps. That is the fidelity to expect from the release law as planned. Sort the table by Change to find the gauges where it falls short.
text.CHECK5: A joint run with a learned release on every dam has to lift the dam gauges clearly above the controls: median per-gauge change in test NSE above zero with its 95 % interval clear of zero, dam gain minus control gain positive, and the controls' median test NSE within 0.01 of 0.761. This offline fit (+0.017 at dam gauges, +0.014 over controls, 210 of 314 up) is roughly the ceiling for a per-dam bucket on this inflow; a release predicted from dam attributes should land between zero and it.
text.CAVEATS: Caveats. The fit uses the routed flow at the gauge as the dam's inflow, which is closest to exact for the 214 dams on the gauge's own reach. Each bucket is chosen on a grid (T₀ from 0.05 to 1,000 days; a and b from −2 to 2): 3 dam gauges hit the 1,000-day wall, and 102 of the 246 dam gauges with an active bucket have a or b on the ±2 edge, so the fitted seasonal swing is often as wide as the grid allows. The fit maximises NSE, and KGE falls slightly at both dam gauges and controls. Rio Hondo below Diamond A Dam (no-dam NSE −17.5) would dominate any mean, so every summary here is a median. The drainage-area match is loose above about 1,500 km² (Figure 2).
